utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everyone. If the witness could take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. If you could make yourself comfortable. Sir, before you begin your testimony, I would like to inform you on behalf of the Chamber that you will be testifying today with the benefit of pseudonym and image distortion. This means that there will be no reference to your real name or information that might reveal your identity to the public or media. The audiovisual record of your testimony which is broadcast to the public will have a distorted image, which can be seen right now in front of your monitor. Why don't you show the image of the witness to the witness. Yes. To ensure that your identity is protected and the transcript, while available to the public, we'll always refer to your pseudonym which is KDZ-379. Yes, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, witness.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could I please have 65 ter 90276.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Witness, on the screen in front of you, could you confirm that you see your name.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd like to tender that pseudonym sheet under seal, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P3331, under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, is it correct that you testified before this Tribunal in the trial of Milorad Krnojelac?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Have you recently had an opportunity to listen to an audio recording of your testimony in that trial?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Do you adopt that testimony as your evidence in this trial, and would you provide the same evidence to the Court if questioned on the same matters here today?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to tender the transcript of the witness's testimony which is 65 ter 22162, for admission as a public exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will be admitted as Exhibit 3332.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I now propose to read a brief summary for the public of the evidence in that transcript. In April 1992, at a JNA fuel warehouse in Filipovici, Foca municipality, the witness and others gave refuge to Muslim civilians who came there from their villages and from the town of Foca to seek protection. They said that an attack had taken place on villages around Foca as well as in Foca town, and people had been expelled. On 26 April 1992, several days after the witness had received a warning from an SDS representative, Pero Mihajlovic, not to offer protection to any more refugees, the fuel depot was attacked and taken over by around 20 armed members of a Serb military formation known as the White Eagles, accompanied by an armoured vehicle. The refugees were placed on a bus and the witness was arrested and taken to Velecevo women's prison. He was shown to a room in which a number of Serb men were having a meeting, including Velibor Ostojic. There were large topographic maps on a table in front of them marked in red and blue, and a large map of Foca on the wall. Ostojic asked the witness if he had joined the balijas and the Ustasha. The witness was then detained at KP Dom in Foca where he saw the bus which had taken the refugees from the warehouse at Filipovici. He testified about the detention of non-Serb women and children at KP Dom. During his detention at KP Dom, the witness was repeatedly returned to Velecevo women's prison for interrogation. That concludes the summary. I'd now like to call up 65 ter 07473, if we can look at the first page in English and B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, as we will see in a moment we will see the first page of an issue of the Official Gazette of the Serbian Municipality of Foca. This issue, as we can see, is dated the 17th of September, 1992. Now, I'd like us to turn to page 8 in B/C/S and page 39 in English. If we could enlarge the top half of the page in B/C/S, please. Mr. Witness, can you see there a record of a decision of the Assembly of the Serbian Municipality of Foca taken on the 3rd of April, 1992, to establish the Crisis Staff of the Serbian Municipality of Foca? Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Can I ask the Registrar to focus on the list of names numbered 1 to 15, on the right-hand side of the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: In that list of names in front of you, Mr. Witness, could you identify by name and number which of those persons you saw at Velecevo on the 26th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: Under number 1, then number 5, number 4, and number 13.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: For the record, number 1 is Miroslav Stanic, number 4 is Vojislav Maksimovic, number 5 is Petko Cancar, number 13 is Radovan Mandic. Simply to clarify the record, Mr. Witness, in your statement of the 23rd of December, 1995 - no need to bring it up for the moment - you referred to a man called Rajko Mandic, who you saw at Velecevo women's prison. Could you confirm whether Rajko Mandic is the same person as Radovan Mandic?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: This doctor was short, but I heard the name, and they referred to him as doctor. But there was another doctor, Crni, but I don't know his proper name and I don't know who the man was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: But you're quite sure that Radovan Mandic was at Velecevo women's prison on the 26th of April 1992?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: I think he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd like to tender that edition of the Official Gazette of the Serbian Municipality of Foca, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That is admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P3333, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd like now to play a video, and this is 65 ter 40199. It was formerly recorded under the number 45314. I'll play a number of clips from this video. If we could start, please, at 4 minutes and 27 seconds. I'd like to direct the interpreters to page 1 of the transcript in English and B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Host: It is three years from the liberation of Srbinje. The guest in our studio is Miroslav Stanic, member of the Main Board of the Serbian Democratic Party of all Serbian states, member of the Municipal Board of Srbinje and the first commander. Welcome."

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Stop there, please. We stopped at 4 minutes and 52 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: First of all, witness, the presenter there referred to Srbinje. What was Srbinje formerly known as?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: Foca.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: What do you understand the term "Srbinje" to denote?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: Well, mostly during the war and after the war, names were changed. All the places that came to belong to the Serbian Republic were changed and they were given other names, with the prefix Serbian, Srpski Brod, Srbinje, and so on. Now, they -- the reason was probably that the Serbs remained in Foca, so that's why they had the place names changed to reflect that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: The second clip will start at 9 minutes and 45. For the benefit of the interpreters, this is at the top half of page 3 in English and in B/C/S. If we could play it, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Host: You were the first war commander in the area of Srbinje. Can you give our viewers your account of the beginning of the armed conflict and the three war years? "Stanic: I cannot talk about the whole period. I shall talk only about the part when I was the commander on behalf of the SDS which enabled me to become the first war commander because I was there at the time. However, I must say, before we continue, our response to their bacchanal in the Drina valley which was inevitable, at least a verbal response, was the magnificent founding assembly of the SDS in September 1990 followed by a yet more magnificent Trojcindan Sabor, or convention, when we said that the Drina would never become a border but a windpipe between two lungs."

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Stop there please. It's stopped at 10 minutes and 40 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. Witness, in that extract Stanic said: "I was the commander on behalf of the SDS, which enabled me to become the first war commander." Now, is that statement consistent with your understanding of his role in Foca in April 1992?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: His duty was the main person, the number 1 man, and I received the information from my colleague who was a prominent public figure and he told me that he was the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Stanic refers to the Drina, and he refers to a statement made at a convention where it was said, "The Drina would never become a border but a windpipe between two lungs." Could you assist us with what you understand that expression to mean?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ask that -- I have to intervene with the translation. He didn't say "granica," a border, he said "medja." There is a slight difference in the terminology dividing -- for example, "medja" is used to divide two fields, the boundary line or dividing line, and I'd like the witness to confirm that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, witness, could you, in any event, explain your understanding of the words used by Stanic and his reference to the windpipe between two lungs?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: Well, one part of the lungs was Serbia, the Republic of Serbia, and the other lung; the other part of the lungs, was Drina, which was to become joined with the Serbian Republic; and on the other side, the other lung would be the people from the Serbian Republic, which meant that they would breathe with the same breathing system, the Serbs on the one side and the Serbs on the other side. They would breathe together.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd now like to move to 15 minutes and 47 seconds. For the benefit of the interpreters this is in the middle of page 4 in English and the lower portion of page 4 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Host: ... knew what the enemy were up to. "Stanic: Of course. What else could I have ordered because experience taught us that if we choose the first option, we would suffer the same fate as Gorazde. That was the beginning of our outstanding victories. We liberated the town in six days. By the 25th of April, we managed to liberate the whole of the Foca municipality, the largest municipality in Republika Srpska. I submitted my war report to the ministerial council, as it was then called at that time, at the beginning of June. We were active in the Crisis Staff, crisis committee, and later in the army command. I turned over the command to 11 officers headed by Colonel Marko Kovac. Our organisation changed names, it was called Tactical Group Drina, and then the garrison. It changed names several times, but the structure of the battalion remained the same until a year ago. It was very efficient, as everyone knows, in the whole of Republika Srpska territory."

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Stopped at 17 minutes, 24 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: In that extract, Mr. Witness, Mr. Stanic referred to the liberation of the town and the liberation of the municipality of Foca in April 1992. On the basis of what you observed, what did the liberation of Foca municipality involve?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: Well, it stretched right to Filipovici, Ustikolina, Jabuka up at the top, and those villages there which belonged to the Municipal Assembly of Foca at that time. They weren't taken control of. It was only on the 26th or 27th when that happened. Up until the 25th, all the rest of Foca municipality had been taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you. And where he talks about -- where he says "We managed to liberate the whole of Foca municipality," what did you understand the liberation process to involve?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: It included the expulsion of the Muslim population from that region, expulsion, killings and incarceration. So it was liberated from the Muslim population of the Municipal Assembly of Foca.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Did you say, "The Muslim population of the Municipal Assembly of Foca"?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: Yes, yes. The Muslim population living in the Municipal Assembly of Foca.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Witness, earlier you identified for the Trial Chamber several members of the Crisis Staff who you saw at Velecevo on the 26th of April, 1992. In the interview, Mr. Stanic has referred to the Crisis Staff and to the army command in the takeover of Foca. Could you comment as to what Stanic's words were and whether they were consistent with what you observed in Foca in late April 1992?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: At that period, the Crisis Staff was the body which assigned war assignments. Since -- well, it issued orders and tasks to some units, whether it was the infantry or some other units that existed. So the Crisis Staff was the body that issued commands to take certain territory, places and positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd like to move now to 18 minutes and 50 seconds. This is the middle of page 5 in the B/C/S transcript and the top of page 5 in the English. To play from 18 minutes and 50 seconds to 19 minutes and 33 seconds.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Stanic: However, I would like to say something about the surroundings of our command, but as far as the Serb sentiments are concerned ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: For the record, witness, could I ask you to read out the words on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: Miroslav Stanic, member of the Main Board of the Serbian Democratic Party, president of the municipal board of Srbinje and the first war commander. So he was a member of the Main Board of the SDS, that's number 1. Then he was president of the municipal board of Srbinje, number 2. And the first war commander, under 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Witness. That was at 19 minutes and two seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Can we play on, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Stanic: I can't say who is a bigger Serb or a better Serb. However, regarding their revolutionary fighting spirit, if certain individuals have been in the command at the beginning of the conflict, we would certainly not be sitting here in free Foca, and we would probably have a constant headache from the muezzins' singing from the tops of the minarets and songs such as 'Vino piju age Sarajlije,' a traditional Muslim song."

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you. We stopped at 19 minutes and 35 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And there we see Mr. Stanic referring to if other Serbs had been in charge, that one might experience in Foca a constant headache from the muezzin singing from the tops of the minarets, what happened to the minarets in Foca municipality after the Serb takeover?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: They were shelled, the minarets were shelled so that most of the mosques were destroyed or had their minarets destroyed. And I was told that by the refugees who came to the warehouse.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Is Mr. Stanic's comment consistent with the conduct of the Serb authorities towards the Muslim population in Foca in April 1992?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could we move now to another clip. This is at 47 minutes and 38 seconds, and this is a speech given by Mr. Stanic to the public, so we will play the introduction to the speech to understand the context in which it was given and then we'll play part of Mr. Stanic's speech. Start now from 47 minutes and 38 seconds. This is on the last page of the transcript, for the benefit of the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "The Reporter: The atmosphere today in Srbinje was magnificent. With the participation of several thousands of citizens of Srbinje neighbouring municipalities, a meeting of support was organised for Dr. Radovan Karadzic, President of Republika Srpska, and General Ratko Mladic, Chief of the Main Staff of the Republika Srpska army. The name of the meeting was: 'We won't give you our Nemanjics without bloodshed,' a verse from Serbian epic, and it was aimed against the provisions of The Hague Tribunal which had charged them for alleged war crimes. The meeting was organised by the municipal board of the Serbian Democratic Party. Besides the representatives of Srbinje municipality, the following prominent people attended the meeting: Zoran Vujanovic, vice-president of the Serbian Democratic Party of Republike Srpska; Bozidar Vucurevic, mayor of Trebinje municipality; Mirko Mijatovic, deputy of the People's Assembly of Republika Srpska; Dr. Dusko Kornjaca, mayor of Cajnice municipality; and Drago Pejovic, deputy in People's Assembly from Cajnice and others. Miroslav Stanic, president of the Municipal Board of the SDS in Srbinje was the first to greet the participants of the meeting, the citizens of Srbinje and neighbouring municipalities. "Stanic: Dear brothers and sisters, dear guests, I would like to greet you all with a sincere wish that there be no more war, but with firm resolution to be the creators of our happiness and our own future. The younger generations do not remember, but those of us relatively older or very old know full well that we organise meeting of support for Patrice Lumumba, Che Guevara, the Karinthian Slovenes, the Czechoslovakians, the Khmer Rouge and many others whose names are almost unpronounceable. So why not support ourselves today? We want to choose our own leaders. We, the Serbs on the west bank of the Drina River, know full well that our leaders are Dr. Radovan Karadzic and General Ratko Mladic."

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Stop there, please. We've stopped at 49 minutes and 40 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: You heard there Mr. Stanic describe the leaders on the west bank of the Drina River as Dr. Radovan Karadzic and General Ratko Mladic. Could you tell the Trial Chamber who, on the basis of your observations, you understood the Serbs of Foca considered their leaders to be in April 1992?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: The Serbs considered as their leader Radovan Karadzic. They saw him as -- or rather, the man number 2 was Ratko Mladic, and that could be seen in various gatherings, rallies. And even before Foca was taken, a colleague of mine who was near another warehouse, he would go on a daily basis to the Municipal Assembly, where there was Miroslav Stanic, and he would get information there which he later conveyed to me. He would describe the situation to me exactly as it was developing. He would tell me what would happen, when, who was their ideological leader, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I've no further questions for this witness. There are no associated exhibits to be tendered. I would like to tender the video in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did you give us the indication as to the time frame of this video, the first interview and this speech?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, from what we have been able to determine, the introduction to the first interview is described as the third anniversary of the Serb takeover of Srbinje, so we would date that as approximately April 1995. The second video, the speech of Mr. Stanic to the crowd, has taken place after the indictment of Radovan Karadzic and Ratko Mladic, which would place it, at the very earliest, in late July 1995, and I don't have any more specific information as to the date of the speech by Stanic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And you are tendering these video-clips in one go, in one exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, we can do that. If Your Honours wish to assess the video-clips in the context of the entire video, perhaps Your Honours might wish to admit the entire video. I leave it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will admit only those parts shown to the Chamber. Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, we object to the portions of the video other than that of the speech because we believe that this is an after-the-fact statement of the third party which you have consistently not admitted. So even though it's oral as opposed to written, this is a 1995 interview, three years after the events, and we believe that it's the same as if it were a written statement taken in 1995 from Mr. Stanic. So it's our position that those -- while the witness's answers and the -- it's a third party statement being shown to a witness. He can comment on it, but we don't believe that under your rules it's admissible. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: When we referred to a third party statement, we usually referred to a news clipping or a newspaper article, interview or the statements taken for the purpose of criminal investigation, et cetera. Do you see any difference taken spontaneously or contemporaneously? Take your time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, there is a difference. There is a difference. Had this been taken in 1992, then we wouldn't be objecting, but it was a contemporaneous -- it was three years after the events. It was reflecting back. The only difference was it was a newscaster instead of some other -- a police officer or investigator from the OTP who was asking someone for their recollection of events which had occurred in the past.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. President, I've prepared some submissions on the matter if you would care to hear them now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Well, first of all, Mr. Robinson is drawing an equivalence between a statement prepared for the purposes of an investigation or for the purpose of testimony prior to a trial, but if you -- the jurisprudence of the Tribunal is consistent that Rule 92 bis and Rule 92 ter and 92 quater are concerned solely with the admission of statements prepared for a criminal investigation or for criminal proceedings. And the principal decision in which the purpose of Rule 92 bis is considered is the decision on interlocutory appeal concerning Rule 92 bis(c) of the 7th of June, 2002, by the Appeals Chamber in the Galic trial, and paragraphs 28 to 31 make it absolutely clear that Rule 92 bis was intended to cover documents made in relation to pending or anticipated legal proceedings. Now, Rule 92 ter which was enacted after Rule 92 bis falls into the same category. Your Honours have provided guidelines to the parties in this case. I'm referring to the additional guidelines which were handed down on the 19th of May, 2010, the decision on guidelines for the admission of evidence through witnesses. At paragraph 25 of that order, Your Honours have set down the additional guidelines. Guideline 25(e) concerns the circumstances in which a party may confront a witness with the witness statement or the transcript of prior testimony of another witness from another case before the Tribunal, so 25(E) is concerned exclusively with proceedings before this Tribunal. Of course, those are general guidelines and Your Honours have also taken a consistent position that documents taken by, for example, RS MUP authorities during the war are documents prepared in the course of a criminal investigation and therefore fall within the general prohibition on using a witness to get around the lex specialis of Rule 92 bis, 92 ter or 92 quater. Your Honours' additional guidelines do set out the general rule which is that a party should tender a piece of evidence through a witness who is either the author of that piece or who can speak to its origins and/or content. The tendering party shall demonstrate some nexus between the witness and the document before offering the document into evidence. You've also ruled that there will be no blanket prohibition on the admission of evidence simply on the grounds that the purported author of the evidence has not been called to testify. Now, in this case, there is clearly no prohibition the admission of this evidence simply because the TV interviewer or Mr. Stanic have not been called to testify. The question is whether we have demonstrated, first, that it is relevant and probative. In my submission, it's relevant because it concerns the circumstances of the takeover of Foca in April 1992. It's probative because it advances the Prosecution's case that the takeover was co-ordinated, among others, by the Crisis Staff and the military, and that it advances the Prosecution's case that the purpose of the takeover was to rid Foca of its non-Serb population. Furthermore, the witness was present in Foca at the relevant period. He observed members of the Crisis Staff of Foca attend a meeting on the evening of the 26th of April, 1992, at Velecevo and the -- that evidence corroborates what Stanic said about the takeover of Foca being more or less complete by the 25th of April, 1992. What Stanic says about the co-ordination between the army and the Crisis Staff in the takeover, and also what Stanic says in relation to, you know, ridding Foca of the annoying sound of the muezzin singing from the minaret. So in my submission, the witness is clearly in the right place, and with his career background, he's qualified to comment on military matters, and we have demonstrated a sufficient basis --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. He's reading into it. This was not uttered. If Mr. Gaynor is testifying, then it's another matter but that's not what we heard from the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. President, I haven't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Don't intervene while the other party is making its submission.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And when am I going to cross-examine Mr. Gaynor?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. He's not giving his evidence. Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. In short, the relevant rule governing the admission of this evidence is Rule 99(c). The question is: Is it relevant? Is it probative? And has the Prosecution demonstrated some nexus between the witness and the evidence before offering it into evidence? And in my submission, the answer to those three questions is yes. For that reason, it should be admitted. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, maybe Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Maybe Mr. Tieger can back me up on this, but it's my recollection that we've already dealt with this identical issue in another instance where video interview after the fact was taken, and I believe that you ruled that that was not admissible, that that was a statement of a third party. I don't know if Mr. Tieger recalls that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Actually do I recall that, Mr. President, because if we are thinking about the same instance, because I believe at that time I had raised a concern that this matter was belatedly raised, and had asked for such matters, such objections, to be raised previously or as early as possible so we could research the matter more fully, and Mr. Robinson raised the same objection. Thereafter, I had the opportunity to go back and see the history behind this objection and discovered that in May of 2010, a similar issue had arisen, that is a videotaped interview that was proffered by the Defence and argued by Mr. Robinson that the witness had provided a sufficient nexus to the comments on the interview, that it had confirmed his basic knowledge of the person who was giving the interview and had purported to affirm some of the underlying statements and that document was admitted at Mr. Robinson's instance. So it's true that this was raised before. I had raised concerns about the fact that we didn't have an opportunity to fully look at the back drop to it, and when I did, I found that the opposite was true, that the Defence had taken the contrary position previously when it was a matter -- when it was a document they wanted in. I don't think there is any question but that the factors outlined by Mr. Gaynor are accurate. We -- his position is completely correct with respect to the proffer here. I would also note that this is the kind of document that would be appropriate, in my submission, for bar table submission by virtue of the fact that we have an executor of SDS policies talking about the reason why those policies were implemented. It's hard to imagine, in fact, more relevant and probative information on its face for the Trial Chamber to consider. So for many reasons, we would assert this document is fully admissible, not the least of which is that that's the position taken by the Defence when this issue was first broached and now that it's a document they don't want in, they have taken a contrary position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just for food for thought, Mr. Gaynor, do you see a difference between the situation in which the witness confirmed the content of the interview and in the case in which the witness did not?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: In my submission, I believe in both cases, the words of Stanic would be admissible. The reason being this: If we had asked a witness, not necessarily this witness, Did you see Mr. Stanic on television, he said, Yes, and we said, What did he say? And the witness then recounted to the best of his memory what the witness had said, that hearsay evidence would be admissible under the Rules of this Tribunal. Now, what we have here is the original recording of Stanic's words, so Your Honours have an opportunity to observe Stanic himself, listen to every single word that he said in the original, which is a far more reliable version of what he said, than simply asking a witness what he had said. For those reasons I believe that whether the witness agrees with what Stanic said is accurate or whether he takes the view that it is inaccurate, it is admissible in both instances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, if I could add to that slightly. It may depend on the position of the declarant. So if the declarant, as in this case, is an SDS official outlining the policy of the party as it was pursued, that has its own independent value, that doesn't require, I would say, a witness to affirm his own independent observations of the reflections of that policy on the ground in contrast to another witness who is not so positioned and whose declarations don't, on their own, have such a powerful probative value.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, can I just make one more small reply. Just thinking about yesterday, you remember when we had the document where this Commander Alagic had been interviewed in 1993 about events in Sanski Most that had taken place in 1991, it was interview by someone in Republika Srpska, and first of all, you chastised Dr. Karadzic for putting the third party statements to a witness. That statement had actually said that the witness was involved in persuading him -- or, it referred directly to the witness's conduct during the events, and you didn't admit it over objection by the Prosecutor because it was a statement of a third party and it was taken after the fact. It wasn't contemporaneous. And that's been basically the rule. We didn't really even complain about that. Now the Prosecution wants to change the rule and have you admit statements of people after the fact that are not contemporaneous and I don't see any basis for changing the rules of the game in mid-stream. How many times have you told Dr. Karadzic, Call this witness, call Prlic, call this one, as a response to when he's putting third party statements to a witness and we asked for them to be admitted. It's time to tell them, Call Stanic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. President, can I make two responses to that, with your leave. First of all, the vast majority of statements put by Mr. Karadzic to witnesses are witness statements taken by investigative authorities. The second point is this, and it may not necessarily apply to the documents Mr. Robinson has just raised, and that is some of these statements put by Mr. Karadzic to witnesses are witnesses taken by RS MUP investigators of Muslim prisoners of war during the conflict, and there has been considerable evidence provided to the Chamber about the interrogation methods used by the RS MUP during the conflict, and such statements may well be inadmissible under Rule 95. But as a general matter, we are not asking the Trial Chamber to change the rules. We are stating that a television interview of a person does not fall within the lex specialis of Rule 92 bis or 92 ter, and it falls within 89(C) 6c and should be considered in accordance with the guidelines that the Trial Chamber has handed down. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber wishes to issue a more informed decision on this, and we will put this matter under its advisement. We will come back to this issue in due course. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, are you ready to start your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, your Excellencies. Good afternoon, your Excellencies, good afternoon to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, witness.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would like to cover as quickly as possible the issues you discussed in examination-in-chief. So, Mr. Ostojic, according to you, objected about you being among Ustashas, had his exact words were that were you among Ustashas and balijas. Is it true that Mr. Izetbegovic knew exactly which faith you were of and what ethnicity you were of, and that that did not mean automatically that you were to be among Ustashas?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: I have nothing to do with Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: No, no. I meant Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: Well, Ostojic said, You went and are now among Ustashas and balijas. And I told him that I was with the JNA and I had nothing to do with the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you, do you know that Mr. Ostojic was married to a Muslim woman and that he never ever used the word balija? (redacted) and there was an unpleasant situation. I know that his wife was a Muslim. I also knew who his father was because that's what I learned from my late father. But these are the words that he addressed to me. He personally said that to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We saw that the Crisis Staff, the Serb Crisis Staff, was established on the 3rd of April, 1992. Do you know when the Muslim Crisis Staff was set up in Foca?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: As an active military serviceman, I was never interested in when the SDS Crisis Staff was set up, nor that one of the SDA, or of any other party in Bosnia-Herzegovina or in the former Yugoslavia for that matter. As an active military serviceman, I received orders from the 777th Logistics Base in Sarajevo which in turn received its orders from Belgrade. So I was not interested in these things in the least. However, my colleague, who was some 3 kilometres away at another warehouse, up until the 2nd of April, he went on a daily basis to the Municipal Assembly in Foca where there were members of the SDA and SDS party. There was the Crisis Staff there as well, or members of the Crisis Staff were present, mostly it was Stanic, this is what my colleague told me. They tried to calm the tensions and to ensure that a war would not break out and that they would find peaceful solutions to the problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know whether -- do you think that all of those members of the Crisis Staff whose names were on the list shown to you by Mr. Gaynor, do you think that all of them are members of the SDS or perhaps some were not?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: There are still political parties in Bosnia-Herzegovina and the SDS is one of them. Currently, it is possible for somebody of another ethnicity to be a member of the SDS. I can give you an example of Desnica [phoen], who is now a member of the SDA and I know another Serb from Sarajevo who is a member of the SDA. However, at that time I didn't know about these matters, I wasn't interested, and I never heard that somebody of another faith could have joined the SDS or the SDA for that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What I wanted to ask you is this: Whether all members of the Serb Crisis Staff were necessarily members of the SDS as well, or perhaps there were some Serbs there who were members of another political party. That's what I asked you.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: Well, the Crisis Staffs depended on political parties, and how they envisioned them. There wasn't just the Army of Republika Srpska during the war but there were also people who remained there after the 29th of May who used to be active members of the JNA -- or rather, the Army of Yugoslavia and then there were members of the paramilitary formations who used to come from Serbia who were not members of political parties, so it doesn't mean that members of the Crisis Staff were necessarily members of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that Foca, before the arrival of Turks and for a while after the Turks arrived, had a different name? Do you know what name it had?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: I don't know. I would probably make a mistake if I were to tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, I will give you a proposition. Do you agree that it was called Foca -- Hoca?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And there is a place name, identical place name, in Kosovo. It exists as well?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: Well, that was a transit town in Turkish times. I've heard of that name, but I never really researched it and I really never was interested in the meanings of words and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said today that Serbs gave Serb prefix to place names. Are there perhaps Bosnian prefixes that remain, for example, Bosanska Krupa, and so on? So were there places that had in their name Bosnian prefix and that -- were such cases known to you and were they also similarly places where Serbs lived and where Serbs added Serbian prefix?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: Yes. It's true. In the old Yugoslavia, there were place names that had prefix "Bosanski" or "Bosnian." And before this war ended, some place names were changed. In cases where Serbs had taken up that territory, they assigned their own names to places based on their own decisions which were published in the Official Gazette and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that during the Austro-Hungarian empire, we and Croatia were part of the same country called Austro-Hungarian empire?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that a number of towns on the Sava River were a single entity, Kostajnica was one town, and then after the Austro-Hungarian empire fell apart, it split into two parts, the Croatian part and Bosnian part. And the same could be said of Brod and Samac and some other places; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you distinguish between the commander of the Crisis Staff and commander of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: The commander of the Territorial Defence could exist in a certain territory, whereas the commander of the Crisis Staff could be in charge of several areas, not necessarily just one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember that Mr. Stanic mentioned the following: He said, Had we not done that, we would have experienced the same thing we experienced during World War II? Do you agree that the Serbs and Muslims exterminated each other in World War II and that Foca was a particularly bloody spot during that war, civil war --

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Objection, this is irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: -- and religious war?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think it's irrelevant. On the basis of that, things happened in 1992 on the basis of the experience gained beforehand and the witness -- or rather, Stanic mentioned that. That is what we believe, that this war was a continuation of the Second World War. That is what we fully believe and the witness can say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In the clip, Mr. Stanic referred to that experience. So for clarification, that question can be asked and answered. Could you answer the question, Mr. Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please repeat that question again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that during the Second World War, the Serbs and Muslims had a terrible experience exterminating each other? What was particularly drastic and bloody was the past of Foca?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: My father, my late father, was a veteran. Foca suffered after the fall of the Drina bridge that had been destroyed. The entire population of Foca fell victim to the Chetniks. Most of these Chetniks came from Montenegro and from Serbia. I can say that the families of Popovic, Dragovic from Foca, who were locals from Foca, they were not in those units, rather they were in the Partizan units. So that statement is not correct. It's not correct that the Serbs and Muslims were slaughtering each other during the war. It was the Chetnik units that were slaughtering the Muslim people. And along with the Muslim people, all of those who were helping them, the Muslim people, or rather, who were against the Chetniks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I allowed you to put that question but if you pursue that line, there is no end. So come to the issues.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, Excellency. I didn't want to establish whose fault it was, but it's a well known thing that the Muslims first sided with the Ustashas, and that was the reason why the Chetniks sought their revenge, and the gentleman, the witness, expanded on this topic. I just wanted to say who did what to the other side without trying to establish who was guilty.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sir, do you know who Alija Siljak is? During this war and before the war, was he not a citizen of Foca who was in the Ustasha movement of the Croatian rights movement in Zagreb? Was he not the vice-president or something like that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: Alija Siljak? I was born in Foca. He's a neighbour of mine. His father and his entire family, one brother and several sisters, are die-hard Muslims. Alija was an extremist who went to Croatia, and he says that he's one of the greatest Ustashas. He's a man with a criminal record, and he had nothing in common with his parents. Quite simply, he strayed away from his own people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that during the war in Croatia, and before our war, quite a few young Foca Muslims went to Alija Siljak to take part in combat against Serbs, to train and to bring weapons? If you didn't know anything about it you can say so, just tell us.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: I did not know about that because I was not in Foca at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know how the negotiations on the transformation of Bosnia were going in order to have the Serbs accept Bosnia's independence and how the negotiations went at the level of the republic and at the level of Foca, and that it was envisaged that there would be two municipalities, one Serb and one Muslim in Foca?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: Since at that time I hardly ever watched the news and followed that, because I was in Pale for a while, but then I was immediately seconded to Filipovici, so I wasn't really interested in this political aspect, whether the division would go this way or that way, or whether things would happen the way they actually did in Sarajevo, that there is this eastern Sarajevo and whatever else. I was not really following all of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it not true that to this day, there is a Muslim municipality that is called Foca Ustikolina?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: Yes. There is Ustikolina who is 12 kilometres away from Foca. That is where the population is Muslim, that is to say the population that was expelled from Foca and from around Foca. The real citizens of Foca rebuilt their houses, do not want to have them sold. That's what they have been saying. Quite simply, they want to have their own homes in Foca. Quite a few real Focaks returned to Foca, but only elderly people. Young people haven't returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know or do you not know that gunfire came from the mosques in Foca, sniper fire, and also fire from heavy weaponry?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: This is some information that you received from someone, and that is not correct. My colleague who went every day to attend meetings did not provide that kind of information to me. We were together until the 25th of April. The 25th of April. That could not have happened until the 25th of April. In addition to that, all the weapons that people had at their homes were handed over in order to avoid a fight. I, as a unit, I didn't have any snipers. How could the Muslims have snipers or somebody else. If the JNA did not have snipers in that territory, how could somebody else? Well, perhaps they may have gotten them from somewhere but I don't know. I haven't heard about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know who Meho Karisik nicknamed Kemo is?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Haven't you heard that he's a general of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina? At the time he was the Commander-in-Chief of the Patriotic League. Meho Karisik, a famous person, a celebrity, have you not heard of him?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: I heard of him in Sarajevo but I thought that you were not talking about that period, April. I mean Meho Karisik was in Sarajevo, although after that, I mean, after Foca I didn't go to Sarajevo so I cannot say exactly who this man was. I heard the name, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This is what Mr. Karisik said in the "Oslobodjenje" daily on the 3rd of May, 1997, on page 21: Just before the war, I was in Foca twice. Foca had quite a lot of weapons. Why was -- were these weapons not used? We are going to find out later who the culprit was. Secondly, we sent two co-ordinators to Foca in order to carry out military preparations for the war. However the people from Foca said that they knew how to do it without them. Probably they mistrusted military personnel. Now you are saying that there were no weapons in Foca, and the general says that Foca had enough weapons. However, they didn't want to accept these officers. What do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Can I object for one moment. The "Oslobodjenje" article that Mr. Karadzic is referring to is not on the list of cross-examination documents referred -- presented to us by the Defence, and if he's going to show it to read large parts of it, perhaps he could show it on the screen to the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I respond? I'm reading this from this book that is called "The black Book," and there is a quote from "Oslobodjenje." I didn't really want to bring this up but the witness denied that the Muslims were armed in Foca. Had he not disputed that, I would not have brought this up. When the time comes, we are going to deal with this through another witness. I just wanted to see whether the witness still claims that Foca had been unarmed. A Muslim general says that Foca had been armed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did you give notice to the Prosecution of the -- your potential use of that "Black Book," Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, no. This is a book that is full of quotations, and it is an accurate quotation. I wouldn't have brought it up had the witness not said something that -- or rather, disputed something that we all knew, or at least I thought we all knew that, we all knew that Foca was armed, and how. I am just reading out to him what the general said in contrast to what he's been saying to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We are discussing the proper disclosure of material you are going to use in your cross-examination. You should give a proper notice to the other party. Consult Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, if the witness is denying something that I did not think he would deny, how do I deal with that? I did not think that that would be denied. It is a generally known thing that Foca was armed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If someone was armed and if that someone is then attacked by somebody else, how come the one who is armed escapes and then Foca falls within six days? So if I have weapons and if I can defend myself and if I have the right kind of morale in my unit, at any rate there has to be fighting. And one part after the other should be liberated or taken or whatever, so the morale in the SDA was zero compared to the SDS that was carrying out the attacks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We have statements from the SDA where it says the entire leadership had fled, Saja, this well known Saja packed up and left. He left people in the lurch. And if the Muslims had been unarmed, the Serbs would not have needed six days to take over. They would have needed only one day; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: Well, maybe. But you know what, well actually you know better than I do, all the Serbs who used to go to school with me who did not want to attack Foca ended up at the KP Dom, the correctional facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, today you mentioned that this person said that he had a headache from the prayer coming from the mosque. Do you know that to this day, there is a recommendation issued by Catholic, Orthodox and Islamic religious leaders that bells should not ring too loud and that prayers should not be called to in this very loud manner either, also discussions were held on having a 50/50 balance. However, to this day, for instance, there is this discussion in Bijeljina because to this day the imam in Bijeljina is playing this call to prayer that is too loud. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: Yes. I know. There is -- there are some situations where the volume is shattering. However, what can we do? People have to come to their senses, and realise that in accordance with their very own religion they should not disturb the other population that lives in the neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know about this incident, or rather, crisis in interethnic relations that broke out in connection with Focatrans before the elections in August and September 1990, when the Serbs lost all rights in Focatrans because that man, Kaliman, the director, did not want to respect their rights? Do you remember that crisis? Did you know about it?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: I knew about it from the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember, or actually, have you heard about this or were you present when the founding assembly was held in -- of the SDS in Foca and I attended, and Mr. Muhamed Cengic attended as well, he is a native of Foca, and together with the Muslim delegation, I threw flowers into the Drina from the bridge where both Muslims and Serbs had been victims before?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: I did not really follow that so I cannot say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me not mention the name of the place that you went to from Pale. You were sent to Foca; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: It was Filipovici that I was assigned to. Not Foca.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Was it your understanding that it would have been a good thing for you to be there in a view of your ethnic and religious affiliation?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: Perhaps that's what they thought but I don't think that that was the thinking of the JNA. On the other hand, this is a purely technical warehouse, and I'm a technical person. So it is only guards that would belong to other parts of the military. As for all the other personnel there, they were technical people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When did you actually arrive there in Filipovici?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: I arrived when the order was written up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What date? If that is a delicate matter we can move into private session.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: It is not delicate at all. On the 15th of January.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The 15th of January 1992; right? Did you live in town or did you live at the warehouse?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: I lived at the warehouse.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: During that time, did you have insight into what was happening in town and in the municipality in general?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: I had no insight until the 2nd of April when in accordance with the orders from our superiors from Sarajevo somebody had to go to Foca. My colleague went, the one who received every -- information every day and, yes, meetings were held and he conveyed all of this to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned in your statements that it was very difficult to get through to Sarajevo. In the beginning of March, there were roadblocks and so on; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And you then thought and said that those were the SDS people; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And what made you think that the SDS had organised the barricades? Where did you get that information from?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: Well, it's not information. It was the actual state of affairs because I was supposed to go back to Filipovici. I didn't go to work, and -- for three days, and when we stopped at the barricade at Trnovo, you knew whose barricade it was. In Miljevina, I had some problems and there were police of -- if it wasn't for the police of the JNA I would have terrible problems. So I knew that there were barricades, people were fleeing towards Montenegro in their private cars, in their firms' cars. They were running to the south.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, these people at the barricades, by the economic school in Sarajevo, you said, and then in other places too, did they have any masks on their faces?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know any of them personally?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And then you said in your statement of the 23rd of December, 1995, which is on page 4 -- or rather, paragraph 4, from April 1996 -- well, you said that you came across the barricades which were erected by the terrorists of the SDS. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: Well, you could say so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, do you equate the Serbs were the SDS? Do you think it's one and the same thing?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: No, God forbid.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You say that in the same statement -- in the same statement of 1995, page 3, paragraph 2, you say there that you came across -- you were stopped at Miljevina by armed SDS people with Chetnik insignia. Did they actually have Chetnik insignia?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: Well, they always did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that at the beginning of April, when the crisis broke out, Professor Koljevic crossed the mountains which were snow-covered, and him and his group were almost shot as -- the vice-president, premier of Republika Srpska, a member of the BH Presidency because they were considered traitors? Did you ever hear about that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: Yes. Those are the kinds of things that happened in wartime. But you couldn't command all the units so that's what happens. So it's not strange. I don't find it unusual.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to raise an objection, I did it as fast as I could. A few moments ago, Mr. Karadzic referred to page 4 of the witness's statement of 1996 which is 65 ter 21 -- 22158, and said the witness had referred to barricades under the control of SDS terrorists, I believe he said. Now those words do not appear in the witness's statement. He says barricades at Mojmilo which was under the control of the SDS. Now, I invite Mr. Karadzic to direct us to where he found the words "SDS terrorists." Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Terrorists of the SDS. And witness confirmed in a way that he can say so. Could you give the reference, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That, then, is footnote 39, and it says the statement of the 23rd of December, 1995. Page 3, paragraph 1. And the statement goes on. The next statement is the 1996 statement, 00391491 is the page number, paragraph 4, and it refers to the barricades at Trnovo by the Treskavica hotel where they had less problems. And then in Miljevina which is the next bit, it's the 1995 statement, page 3, paragraph 2, that in Miljevina, when they arrived there, they found armed SDS people there, they were called Elezi and they had Chetnik insignias; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The issue was whether witness referred to the terminology of terrorists of the SDS. So he's asking for the reference for that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's in that first 1995 statement, page 3, paragraph 1. The 23rd of December, 1995, page 3, paragraph 1. 1D04224 is the number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are you satisfied with that, Mr. Gaynor?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'll check that, Mr. President, and I'll come back to you if there is any issue. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know that the SDA issued, to its followers, instructions and directives to block the JNA barracks and to attack the JNA barracks?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: No. Because I didn't collaborate with the SDA. I just co-operated with -- well, I wanted to call a meeting between the SDS and the SDA twice, representatives from the warehouse, but I didn't succeed in reconciling the two sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, did you happen to note whose barricades in Sarajevo existed, were there only Serb barricades or were there Muslim barricades in Sarajevo too?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: When I was supposed to report for duty in Sarajevo, well, I set out, first of all, towards Trnovo, and I was unsuccessful. The barricade that was there was in the eastern section of Sarajevo, and that was a Serb barricade. The next day, following orders, I was supposed to go across Bascarsija to Pale, but I didn't manage to do that because there was fighting and the tunnel was unsafe. On day three, I tried to go towards Kosmice [phoen] and Trbelic [phoen], but I didn't succeed in doing that either because there was shooting once again. Whether it was from both sides, I can't say, but anyway I went back. On the fourth day, I set out towards Trnovo and that's where I had problems. They asked that the chief of the municipality in Trnovo be replaced so we were stopped. We had a big problem. And the barricades in Trnovo were Serb barricades. In Miljevina there were Serb barricades again. There were no other barricades because I reached the barracks with ten military policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, is it true that the Marshal Tito Barracks is located practically in the centre of Sarajevo, between the museum and the railway station and that it is in the Muslim part of Sarajevo, if I can put it that way?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: Well, yes, that is true. That's its location, proper location. However, you can't say that it's the Muslim section of town because behind the barracks, behind the Marshal Tito barracks, there is a monument to Tito, and to the left of that, and you know this full well, there are some apartment houses where there were active military personnel living, high-ranking officers, in fact, and you know that much better than I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If it is convenient, shall we take a break now?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just ask one more question before we break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it true that you had difficulties, together with Kovacevic, or whoever you were with, to reach the barracks? And is it true that the barracks were blocked by the Muslim forces, the Green Berets and the Patriotic League?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, did you have difficulty in reaching the barracks?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: No. The difficulties I had was in Miljevina, whether they would let us through or not. Because in Miljevina, they picked and chose whether they would let you go towards -- on towards Montenegro because people were fleeing. So I arrived there with the military policemen that I mentioned and they were armed, and everybody setting up this blockade, all of us, the Serbs, the Croats and the military police was under my command, and so there would have been an attack and we would have defended ourselves. So they couldn't stop us because they knew that a clash would ensue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Not even Elezi; right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Gaynor, did you find that the witness indeed in his statement in December 1995 referred to barricades set up by the SDS terrorists?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, I did find that reference, thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will take a break for half an hour and resume at 3.35.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness, is it true that you thought that the military security and military police were surveying you and controlling you?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: I didn't give it much thought.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you said something similar, that you were monitored by the military police in Ustikolina. You say that in your statement of the 20th and 21st of April, 1996, on page 00391491, paragraph 2. Did you think that they mistrusted you?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: Well, if I said that in my statement, then quite possibly yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that for a whole year before the war broke out, the Muslims and Croats did not do their regular military service, nor did they respond to the call-up for reservists, the mobilisation of reservists and the call-up there?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: As far as I know, in Donja Skladiste, next to me, the lower warehouse, the Muslims were reservists and it was only on the basis of an order from the SDA on the 1st of January, 1992, that they all left the JNA as reservists.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you mind?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: No, because I didn't want to accept duties that weren't the duties of regular soldiers so I just had regular soldiers within my composition, I didn't have any reservists so it didn't effect me much, except for my deputy, he was a reservist and a civilian. All the others were soldiers of different ethnicity. I had Albanians, Macedonians, Serbs from Serbia proper, Serbs from Bosnia and Muslims. It was the regular -- well, they were doing their regular military service which was extended for two or three months.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it true that at one point in time, while you were in Ustikolina, the Muslim reservists left the JNA?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: Yes, they did. They left the JNA, that's quite true, and as far as logistics was concerned, I was linked to the lower barracks so I knew exactly what was going on down there in the barracks, and I was on good terms with the commander who was down there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And it was a fuel warehouse, was it not, and other military equipment was stored there as well?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: It was just a fuel warehouse, which following an order given in December from the federal state organs of Yugoslavia, it was transferred for the army, army purposes, for the JNA, and they were -- it was supposed to serve the UN units, supply the UN units in that area. That was the purpose of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. May we have D400 briefly on e-court, please. I'd just like to remind you and ask you whether as an officer, you knew that an order was issued to block the barracks of the JNA units. On the 12th of April was the first one, the second one on the 22nd of April, and the third one on the 29th of April.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: No, I did not know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we take a look at the document now. You have both versions, Serbian and English. And this is dated the 29th of April. So this is from the minister. The minister of internal affairs elaborating the directive given by Hasanefendic. Is it true that on the 8th April, the command of the Territorial Defence of -- Vukosavljevic [phoen], a Serb was replaced and Hasanefendic, a Muslim, appointed in his place? Is that true?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. So I can't say either way. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we -- well, take a look at where it says, I am ordering, I hereby order, that paragraph, so your colleagues from the JNA, did they warn you of it, that this order would be issued? And it was given on the 12th of April. This is an elaboration at the MUP.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: No they didn't draw my attention to that because in Sarajevo at the command, every day at 8.00 we would report, and it was the duty of the commander down there at the barracks to inform others of the information -- the commander in Sarajevo of the information received. So we had to inform and brief Sarajevo every day on events up until the 22nd of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But the telephone lines were down after the 22nd of April; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you able to go to Foca and call from Foca, or were those lines down too?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: Well, communication with Foca were operational, but I didn't need to do that because I was on orders from -- it was the commander from Donja, the lower barracks. He was -- he had orders to go and see what was happening and to report back to the commanders in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, between Filipovici and Foca, the lines were not down, but between Foca and Sarajevo, the communication lines were down; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: I don't know. I think the switchboard, the exchange, was manned by seven soldiers and an officer, senior officer. Now, what happened to that, I'm not sure. My telephone line was not working to Sarajevo or with Foca. So on the 23rd I wasn't able to call Foca either.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, is it true and correct that in the second half of April, a helicopter arrived and a Muslim officer and another Serb lower-ranking officer brought salaries with them?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: Yes. They brought in the salaries, and they bought some sanitary material because the previous day, the helicopter which was supposed to fly in all these medical supplies was stopped in Foca. Anyway, it wasn't -- the medical supplies were not handed over for the purposes of the JNA. So the next door warehouse to me received very little medical supplies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hasanefendic came together in that helicopter with another Serb?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. That's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it true that they came in a helicopter because due to roadblocks and wartime operations, one couldn't travel in a car?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: No. It seems that the itinerary that the helicopter was taking and that was Sarajevo-Pale-Foca-Filipovici-Visegrad and then back to Pale and Sarajevo, Rajlovac, dictated that they come in a helicopter. In such situations when one anticipate something it is quicker and more efficient to travel that way. In addition to that, they received an order from Sarajevo, not from just anybody. There were people in charge of security who were there to evaluate whether transport should be made by this means or by some other means.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That was on 19th or 20th of April and the order came from the JNA command in Sarajevo, the command of the 2nd Military District; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: Yes. That was the 2nd Military District, 777th Logistics Base.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statement, 65 ter 22158, on page 5, paragraph 7, you say that the refugees kept coming into your facility. And that the refugees were threatened by paramilitary groups, not by regular forces. It was you who took in refugees as well as your deputy, Zoran Milicevic. Is this Milicevic a Serb?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: Yes. All soldiers remained faithful to the JNA. My deputy was Zoran, and we took in refugees because there had been an order on the 12th of April saying that we could take in refugees. Prior to that, on the 6th of April, I talked to my superior, Zoran Jovanovic, lieutenant-colonel, in Sarajevo, and he told me that he would be sending me a written order stating that I could house refugees. He also said that he would guarantee in case there was an attack on either of the warehouses, that they would react, that they would evacuate us and the refugees. Since I had no fax machine, the order arrived at the lower warehouse. And later on, I had to show this order when some other forces came to take the barracks, and that saved my life.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you please look at the same page where it says that the Muslims on the 6th of April 1992 started fleeing from Foca to Gorazde, quite a number of them stopped in my warehouse, that's your warehouse, so these are the refugees that had fled town and had come to you, right, already on the 6th of April?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: Yes, yes. No, they actually started coming already on the 3rd of April, the refugees. And they started inquiring whether they could find shelter with me because they still believed, and this is what the SDA was saying and Alija, they were still saying that they were believing in the JNA. So this is why the people came inquiring whether they could spend a night in the barracks, to which I told them they could stay in the houses that were next to the barracks, and that on the following day they could start doing something. I had received a verbal order from my superiors, based on which I took in refugees, I had to confiscate their weapons first, and if they wanted to leave the warehouse and go to Gorazde because one couldn't travel to Sarajevo any longer, one had to travel via a forest, and as they were leaving I would give them back their weapons. They mostly did not have any rifles, just pistols.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So the refugees had some weapons on them and who did they return the weapons to?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: They didn't return the weapons to me. I was duty-bound to take their weapons as they arrived in the warehouse and I kept their weapons while they were staying with me. As they left the warehouse, I would return their weapons to them. It was mostly pistols. You know yourself what one can use a pistol for, only for short-distance firing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you see the next passage where you say in your statement that the Crisis Staff of the SDA, on the 10th of 11th of April, fled from Foca because their life was in danger there? Do you agree and did you know that the Muslim fighters were quite dissatisfied? They wrote reports to Izetbegovic saying that they had been betrayed, that the elite had run away, leaving them to fight the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: President of the Municipal Assembly of Foca, Gojo, who in wartime, in a way, became a commander and was a member of the SDA, he was among the first to flee to Ustikolina. One day, after the landing of the helicopter, I met him for the first time. He came looking for some medical supplies, saying that they had nothing at the health centre in Ustikolina, to which I replied that me and the commander of the other warehouse received basically very little of the medical supplies, which were insufficient for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.
