Do you know that from the -- in the Muslim part of Foca, the hospital was surrounded, that they were firing at the hospital and that the director of the hospital, Dr. Simo Stankovic, informed via Tanjug that there were bullets flying into the hospital, that the surgical ward had been damaged and that the hospital had been practically completely surrounded?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: I was informed about Simo Stankovic from the other commander. I also knew about the case that you described, and when these people came and took all medical supplies from the hospital, I also heard about that. I think that Dr. Simo was almost killed on that occasion and my colleague informed me of all of these events.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that on 8 April, in the evening, there was shooting on the Serb houses and that the house of Dr. Kovac, a dentist, was set on fire, Mico Krnojelac, and some other houses owned by Serbs, that the Green Berets took large parts of town under their control, and that all the way up until the KP Dom, the entire territory was fired at?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: I didn't know all these details, but, yes, the commander told me that there was some shooting on some houses near the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were there any Serbs who had sought shelter in your barracks or was it just Muslims?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: Among the first group of refugees, there was a Serb. He was a relative of a school friend of mine, Stojan. His name was Ivan and he was among the first ones to come. He remained there the entire time until the barracks was overrun.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And did you hear that prior to the conflict erupting, there were a lot of Serbs and Muslims, entire families, who had left Foca and that later on, after the fighting calmed down, the Serb authorities issued a public statement inviting all of them to come back?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: I have heard of that. However, if one wants to be reasonable, if you want to take a reasonable look at it, to return after the territory after having been expelled from there, after the war had taken place there, to return to the place where there were a lot of newcomers from some other areas, regardless of who had control of the area, whether Serbs or Muslims, I wouldn't recommend anyone to come back without there being a stable system in place. And to this day we don't have a stable system in Bosnia, even though it is peaceful.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So you speak about people who had come from elsewhere. You call them paramilitary formations. Do you have the White Eagles in mind when you say that? Those White Eagles were headed by Desimir Dida and some other people who were not from Foca.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: I speak of people who had come in and taken territory. Dida himself said that he had been tasked with doing that. He said that his order was to take up 65 per cent of the territory and to ensure that it was Serbian. Those people were against the Yugoslav People's Army and they wanted to be paid for their services. They also didn't allow anybody to disobey their orders, otherwise they would kill them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it true that you observed, yourself, that they were far more powerful than Krnojelac and some others, and you stated so in your testimony?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: Yes, because that same Dida told me in the office that Serbs from Foca were not good fighters, in his view. Only Serbs from Krajina were good fighters. And as for the other Serbs, he used an insult when referring to them, and this is what I stated in my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it true that the SDA Crisis Staff moved to a factory of carpets; is that right? Was there such a factory?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: Where did you find that written?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, that's something you stated in your statement given on the 20th and 21st April, 1996, 003942, paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Karadzic, he said SDS Crisis Staff, not SDA Crisis Staff on that one.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. It says here, [In English] "They also told him ..." [No interpretation] [In English] "... was functioning from the factory producing carpets and rugs and they started their own radio station."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's upload it. What's the 65 ter number? April 21st.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 22158.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We don't broadcast the first page.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see 391492. Three pages further, or four pages further down. Now, that should be paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which paragraph?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. It says, "I was also told by them that Krizni Stab," I take it Crisis Staff SDS, "was functioning from a factory producing carpet and rugs."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was that the SDS Crisis Staff in the carpet factory or the SDA staff?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: Based on what I heard, they killed a certain number of people, and they mentioned the names, so unless it was a case of the SDA shooting at their own people, I don't think so. They also said that nobody around the railway station had even a theoretical chance of crossing the bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. And it begins with the words that the Crisis Staff of the SDA escaped from Foca and then they say that the SDS was actually in the carpet factory. Do you know who was at the carpet factory?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Very well. So when the refugees arrived in your base, you were cautious, you were worried that White Eagles could attack them; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: I thought somebody could attack them. I was afraid that there would be a situation where the SDA, who was stationed near the fence of the warehouse, could cause some shooting, and on one night there was shooting. So one day I called Suad from the SDA and I told them, We are not going to shoot at you first and make sure you don't shoot at us, otherwise there would be huge problems. Therefore there was never a single incident while the regular army was in place and while the SDA was there up until the 26th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So between the 6th of April until the 26th of April, you hosted those refugees and you provided for them?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: I didn't really host them. That was no hosting. Those people slept on tables, under the tables, I couldn't provide food for them, excuse me, because I received my supplies from the lower barracks. These people stayed in the houses that were next to the warehouse and they found food there, but it was important for those people to be able to spend a night safely at the warehouse making sure that nobody was killed and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was there nevertheless some shooting in the area, shooting between Muslims and Serbs, in the vicinity of your base?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: Yes. There was shooting. I sent out my deputy, Zoran, when two Serbs were killed in Gornji Grad. So I sent out my deputy, Zoran, to see what the situation was, to talk to people, to check with the SDA representative Suljo, what needed to be done. He did all that together with Vukovic, Drago Vukovic. However, there was yet another shooting after that between them, and two more Serbs were killed in that shooting. So all in all, four men were killed up there. And after the other two were killed, the situation escalated and people didn't really talk rationally any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the Serbs suspect refugees of being armed still and did they suspect them of shooting, those refugees who sought shelter with you?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: Which Serbs do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Those who were getting killed in the area, those that were involved in shootouts with the SDA.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: No way. Even the representative of the SDS, Pero Mihajlovic or Knezevic, I don't know, anyway, this was the man who co-operated with me. He phoned me and not at a single moment did he suspect the refugees of having done anything. They were fleeing for their lives. So it's the population of Filipovic together with Novi Grad. So it's both. I mean, nobody involved the refugees in anything and they had nothing to do with any of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, how did your superior command interpret this, the takeover of this base?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: Well, I stated that quite properly in my report, regardless of which report you're looking at. (redacted) (redacted) that the commander from the lower warehouse had found out that there would be a takeover of Ustikolina within six or seven days. In our report we provided this information to our commander. He said that he would take all necessary measures and issue orders to prevent that. However, unfortunately, on the 22nd April, all communications were cut, telephone, telefax, everything, all communications were Sarajevo, so we did not have any contact at all with our commander or did we know what was going on, and which order we should be receiving or not receiving, because telephones and everything else were taken over, but by who, we don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said in your statement, on the 23rd of December 1995, paragraph 4 -- or rather, page 4, paragraph 1, that already on the 25th, the White Eagles, led by this Desimir, Dida, and his brother started attacking the warehouse; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: Yes. Shells were falling. However, you know full well that in war, it depends on what the co-ordinates given for the shells were. So shells were falling on the village and on the warehouse, and later on there was sniper shooting towards the entrance so I actually had to withdraw my soldier from the entrance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your testimony, in the Krnojelac trial, that was page 3109 to 3110, you say that in the night between the 20th and the 25th, the gunfire was getting closer, closer and closer to this warehouse, and that refugees started leaving on the 25th of April during the night. They were going to Gorazde; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: Well, yes. That's what I said but it's been so long, so many years, and you keep insisting on each and every minute detail. Well, I guess you're entitled to do that. But anyway, I've already said that from the 3rd onwards refugees started arriving, and some of them stayed for a day or two and others would just spend the night there and then go on to Gorazde. However, on the 25th, when we knew already, this commander who was close to me -- when we knew that the attack against Ustikolina was being prepared, we said, Run because we cannot guarantee anyone's safety or life. And I don't want people to get killed and I don't want it to be my responsibility. And I'm not to be blamed at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But these were the White Eagles, and in your testimony on page 3112, paragraphs from 2 through 5, you say that at the end they ultimately showed up at the entrance to the warehouse and they were asking for something. They were asking for some negotiations or something?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: No. During that shooting, a soldier brought this sort of piece of paper, before they broke through by the gate. I had to withdraw my soldier from the gate, and before this break through, the soldier came and since I had deployed all the other soldiers -- I mean, if there were to be an attack, we would respond by way of an attack. He was waving this paper, whatever, he was saying that a fax had arrived because the fax machine started working and he said that that was an order, and I said, Come in through the main gate, try to crawl underneath the main gate, and then after five metres, he was supposed to leave his weapons. However, in the meantime there was this breakthrough by the White Eagles with this vehicle of theirs and then the situation was different. They entered the barracks, and I can tell you about all the rest if you're interested.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Then they prevailed; right? There were more of them and they prevailed, and you know exactly that it was the White Eagles. What kind of insignia did they have?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: On their vehicle, it said, the Serb guard, Srpska Garda. Dida then said, "We are the White Eagles." They were marked with all sorts of markings and insignia. Five-pointed stars. However, they had no insignia of the JNA. They had all sorts of badges and whatever else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us see now how this Lieutenant-Colonel Zoran Jovanovic reported to his superiors, the 2nd Military District.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D42160, can we have that for a moment, please. Can we have that in e-court. 1D4260.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, this is his report. Was there a warehouse in Stojkovici, a JNA warehouse? Please take a look at this, the first sentence. Situation in unit 744, logistics brigade.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: I don't know about Stojkovic. I really wasn't interested in that, to tell you the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. He reports here that this warehouse in Stojkovici was taken by some Muslim colonel, Filipovic, or rather, the forces of the Territorial Defence of the BH. And then this paragraph 3, it says that he received a report that this warehouse in Filipovici was taken, and the commander and nine soldiers were taken to the KP Dom Foca by the Crisis Staff of Foca, their forces. This was preceded by the entry of refugees including armed members of the SDA who probably intended to take the warehouse. Aware of this incursion, SDS formations intervened and placed the warehouse under their control, (redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let us proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please, do you see this? Now, down here there is yet another reference to Ustikolina, that there were conflicts, I mean it's this fourth paragraph down here. Now, what does it say here in the fifth paragraph, the commander of the 2nd Military District took measures to have the commander and the soldiers returned to the warehouse, and then the next paragraph, that there was fighting. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And the combat went on from 12 until 1500 hours, between the SDS and the SDA, and he doesn't know who they are, the SDS and the SDA, and he thinks it's the Serbs and Muslims; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So do you see that there was this fear, there was this information that among the refugees there were combatants of the SDA who had sought shelter and that they would take over the warehouse, and that was the reason for the Serbs to break into the warehouse?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: I mean, well, of course, you're entitled to ask whatever you want. Twelve people -- I mean, if all of them were Muslims, those who went to the KP Dom -- since they did not have any weapons because we had frisked them. So they could not have been armed. All the weapons, the pistols, were taken. Only if they threw something over the fence, but there was a soldier who was guarding the fence, two soldiers actually. Now, these 12 people, taking 17 soldiers of mine, who were in the warehouse and that the SDS had to intervene? And my soldiers were combat ready, although they did not have mortars but they had proper side arms. I mean, I really cannot understand any of this. I cannot understand this at all. The 12 men unarmed can take 17 men who are armed and that somebody needs to intervene.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what about these people outside the warehouse? Did they know that it was 12 people or could they think that it was all over and that the warehouse could fall into the hands of the SDA? They had no way of knowing, right, how many of them were there?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: Well, they had had no way of knowing, but there has to be some kind of reconnaissance, some kinds of unit that was reconnoitering, although there was a war, that had to have been monitored by some formation. I mean, please. On the 25th, I've already said that I had said everyone should flee, just to save their lives. They should run for their lives, with their children. I mean, I wasn't interested in anything else. I mean, I didn't belong to any one of these formations and I wasn't interested in any of this, and that's when the warehouse was emptied. It was basically children, old men and women who remained. So these 12 men they could not go any further. They were either sick or quite simply they were not capable of doing anything. Anybody could see the columns that were moving on the 26th, that were leaving in the morning. Everybody who could, left. When the attack started, five or six men with women broke into the warehouse. I have no idea who they were. They sought shelter, there and I put them in a hangar and I have no idea who these people are. It was just a question of saving their lives. I wasn't really interested in anything else, to tell you the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, is it correct that you say, actually, that they were reinforced with another 50 White Eagles who had come on buses, and they looked through the depot, looking for weapons, ammunition, and soldiers who were guarding the warehouse? That's what you said in your statement of the 23rd of December, 1995, on page 4, paragraph 1. Was that actually the case?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: They came. They searched the entire warehouse. They wanted to torch it. And then I had to say where the refugees were. And then I opened all the safes that I could, and then they found those that had not been opened, and then they went to take weapons, ammunition, everything else. I had already issued an order to the soldiers who were under my command, that they should come in front of the headquarters, and they did come and none of them got killed, whereas the Serb guard or White Eagles they were searching through the warehouse. They took everything they could. They loaded all of that and then they left with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So what did they load on those vehicles and what type of weapons?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: Well, if I have to say, I guess I have to say, first of all, I did not have any anti-armour. I had infantry weapons, nothing else. Because according to the order that I had received from Commander Jovanovic, in case there were to be any kind of attack, additional units would arrive and they would be supplied logistically from the third warehouse that was close to me, and that I would receive help in troops from the third warehouse. Perhaps it was three BK for infantry weapons, combat sets.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The interpreters probably don't know what BK is. It's combat sets, kits.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: Yes, yes. And then you use that for firing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Then you and your soldiers were taken away, nine soldiers, it says here, right, your soldiers?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: No. Nine? Seventeen soldiers, not nine soldiers, eight civilians, rather.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Ah-hah. Eight civilians, well, there were 17 Muslims who were taken prisoner and taken to Velecevo together with you; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: They set out towards Velecevo. They were not there. Actually, they went down to Livade. That's what I found out later, that they returned the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And you went on. Who went with you to Velecevo?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: My driver, and Dida was in this other car, and two more people who were from the White Eagles. I don't know who they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And then you say that you saw a map on the table there. Was it on the wall or on the table?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: Both. On the table and on the wall, Vojo Maksimovic arrived then, and he said, I've just come from Belgrade. I don't know about any of this. I saw these topographic maps on the wall, and on the table, and I saw some circles placed around certain locations and I saw red and blue arrows, and I couldn't see any details because I came as a man who was a prisoner.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What you saw in that map, did it correspond to what you had heard that 60 per cent of the territory of the municipality of Foca was Serb and that it belonged to the Serb municipality?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: No, I couldn't. Who could do that? I mean, you're taken prisoner and you're looking at details? I just cast a glance there. And after all, it wasn't 60 per cent of Foca, but I told you a moment ago, 65 per cent of the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina was supposed to be Serb and they did not want the JNA. Perhaps I did not speak properly but that was their main objective. That is why these people were there anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And did you see on the map that there were two areas, one was green and one was blue, the Serb and Muslim areas?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: No. It depends who marks what area in what colour. Whether the units attacking or combat units, whether red or blue or green. No, I can't say. I said I saw topographical maps on the table. I asked, What's this? And I saw them on the wall. I wasn't an idiot. I didn't want to ask about any details, and nobody would have allowed me to ask about the details anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Then you mention Ivanic, for example, who told Stanic to see that nobody killed you, and that there would be refugees and soldiers who were held in the school centre, and that they would be released.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: Yes, that's what Ivanic said. He said I'm a Serb and I have to leave on the 15th of May, otherwise I'll be a POW. And I'll be considered a war criminal unless I leave on the 15th of May. And he said, you mustn't kill this commander here. I'll inform everyone. You have to release the refugees and the soldiers have completed their military service and you have to let them go home. How they are going to get there and what transportation they are going to use is another matter. So Stanic had come out before that and he said that to Stanic, and that was the end of the story.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, bear in mind that you have five minutes left.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'd like to ask Mr. Robinson to present our views in the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, if I could just indicate that the examination which is the subject of the 92 ter is approximately two hours and 50 minutes of direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We observed how he spent one hour or more than an hour on what matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, what has been admitted already as direct examination is far in excess of what you've allowed him, and there was one hour of cross-examination in that case, and that was the case of an individual who had nothing to do with the events in this municipality other than at one specific location, and didn't involve any of the events that Dr. Karadzic has been questioning this witness on. So he ought to at least have the same amount of time as the direct examination which, when added to Mr. Gaynor's half an hour, is about three hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Number 1, that submission was too late. It should have been raised at the outset. And I don't see any good reason to extend the time. But we will consult.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Excellencies, initially we asked for ten hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you have 15 minutes to conclude your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I just wanted to remind you that initially we had asked for ten hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I won't repeat our ruling, we gave it to you, in relation to how we come to the conclusion as to the proper time for your cross-examination. Just get on with it, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness, is it correct that this man Dida was well -- liked to threaten, to say that he would kill the refugees and you, and that he had to be held back by Vlado and Krnojelac, and that Krnojelac said that was an order, that he should leave the refugees alone?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: Dida wanted to kill the refugees at 3.00 a.m., 3.00 at night, because they had failed to pay him something that was due him, and he wanted call up Vojvoda, however, Vlado prevailed, whether it was his cousin or brother or what, not to call him because he would have problems, and then the chief, Milorad, told me that he mustn't do that to the refugees because there would be terrible problems if that were to happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And he also threatened you, said he would kill you, and he was prevented in doing so, once again, by someone?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That someone was Krnojelac, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And he didn't kill any of the refugees, did he?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: Thanks to Krnojelac, who found a method of dissuading him. He talked to him, he told him not to call up Vojvoda, and he said that -- and somehow he managed to send the women and children to the KP Dom and to protect them. How he managed to do that, I don't know, but later on those people left, except for the men, that is. The women and children were allowed to go but not the men. Krnojelac told a young man, I knew that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So they were sent to the KP Dom for one night to save them from Dida's intentions; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Then they ordered the White Eagles to leave Foca; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: Yes, on the 15th of May, otherwise they said they would be considered as war criminals, so anybody who didn't leave until the 15th of May -- a United Nations letter came in, and the deadline was extended to the 29th of May, but after the 29th of May everybody remaining in Bosnia would be considered as a criminal of war. That's how the International Tribunal would see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This man Ivanic, did he link that up to the decision on the JNA's withdrawal from Bosnia, and did he say that after the 15th of May, anybody remaining would not be there legally?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: Yes. That's right. And not only him. There were others in the warehouse, there were some officers, who were from Cacak for instance and from different places, Smederevo, and so on, who left. They left as early as the 10th because they were told from Belgrade to withdraw. So -- and that anybody who failed to withdraw, well, would suffer the fate they would suffer. God help them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it true that these White Eagles threatened to set fire to villages? And I think they did set fire to a Serb villages because one of their members was killed, I think, and that they were quite wild and their actions were unforeseeable?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: When they said what their aim was, well, somebody issued orders to them and said that 65 per cent of BH should be Serbian, and then the soldiers linked up and they said, we will see what we are going to do with the village tomorrow because one of our men was killed. And they would send his body to Serbia to be buried there. And then they said those Serbs will pay, they will pay for that. And then there was a village, I'm not sure of the name of the village, but anyway they did set fire to the village, and the people fled to Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So they didn't differentiate much between the Serbs and Muslims, Serb houses and homesteads and Muslim households?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: Well, according to the order, they were given the assignment, and they were mercenaries, they were paid to carry out those assignments. All they were interested in was to be paid for their assignments.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, did you manage to learn who the man behind the name Vojvoda was?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: No. He was called Motorola, but who he was and what he was, I have absolutely no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, on the 30th of April, or rather, on the 30th of April, from Ustikolina you went -- moved towards Titograd, Titograd which is now called Podgorica, and then further on to Belgrade; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: Yes. Although this isn't important for our discussions, I did go to Belgrade, yes, and I fled from Belgrade and went to Macedonia, and from Macedonia I went to Turkey, and from Turkey I returned to Slovenia, but they are all unimportant details as far as you're concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. But you were interrogated briefly and they were interested in the arming of Muslims, the refugees from Foca and the leaders of the SDA; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: They didn't raise an indictment against you, did they?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: No, they did not. And I was supposed to go to court in Sarajevo first but I didn't want to because I'd have to go through Miljevina and then Ivanic ordered me to go to Belgrade, and that's how things were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know how many of these Elezi were killed during World War II and how many were killed in this war? You mentioned the Elezi as a separate entity, an entity that didn't want to listen to anyone. So do you know how many of them were killed in World War II and then this recent war?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: I know that the partisans killed quite a lot of the Elezi during World War II because -- and lots of them lost their mind through what had happened, but how many in this war, I don't know. They had their command at the exit to Miljevina. I saw it that night. They were in the restaurant. But they were all prominent citizens in Sarajevo. Vojo Maksimovic knows about that. You know about that. All this situation concerning the Elezi, you were all well aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, according to your personal experience as an experienced officer, to what extent did personal revenge and the history of families influence the situation and what happened in Foca?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: As far as the families of Foca are concerned, there would never have been a war. There was just a portion of individuals. Let's take Stanic as an example. He co-operated and collaborated very well with the Muslims. He was on good terms with them. He was on excellent terms with my brothers. Take Vojo Maksimovic, he had an excellent relationship with my brother, and as a professor and a family of long standing, Muslim families, Serb families, they got on very well. Just as Blagojevici in the Old Town, get on well with the other Muslim families. No problem there. However, certain number of extremists who -- and I say extremists because they were people who couldn't resolve these problems and reach an agreement by peaceful means, but resorted to fighting which was to nobody's advantage, I think we would have been able to find a peaceful solution. And none of this would have happened. I think there were enough Serbs in Foca, old-standing Foca families, who would have found a solution. Saja, there was Saja, and well, I can exclude him. But the people of Foca know who these people are and which these old families are and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, do we agree that Sahinpasic, nicknamed Saja, was rather extremist and a fairly well off and able to finance a lot of those SDA operations in Foca?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: Well, I can't say anything for certain but Saja is a man who is interested in money. Money is what he's interested in. And from a green grocer, he grew to become a businessman. And in Sarajevo he had a whole chain of refrigerator trucks, and so on, and you know that arms and drugs yield the greatest profits. You don't need me to tell you that. So just look at him and his situation. He's got a palace now. His brother is a very intelligent man, one of the most intelligent men living in Sarajevo. He -- but he has his own views.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that Saja was the owner of the paper "Vox," which was published before the war and during the war?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: No. I haven't heard of that, no, to be quite frank.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How are these relevant to your case, Mr. Karadzic? You have two minutes to conclude your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, I have to paint the entire picture of the situation in Foca because many witnesses testified to the things that happened to them and that's all. But thanks to the Prosecution, there are a lot of generalised and general things that he has talked about, and I can't discuss these with anybody else but him because it's in his statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And now one last question, witness: Did you know or do you know -- well, it's half my last question: Do you know who Halid Cengic and Hasan Cengic are, men from Foca?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: Halid Cengic was a miller, a deputy miller, but he profiteered, he was a profiteer. The other one I know by sight but I don't know much about him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And Halid Cengic -- Hasan, his son, Hasan Cengic, he's a Muslim priest and a high-ranking official of the SDA, did he appoint from the main quartermaster in Visoko -- do you know that Halid Cengic in August 1990 established the first units of the Patriotic League in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that. I don't know about that. When I was down there, he was an ordinary manual worker. Now, all this about the SDA, I really don't know. I'm not a member of any party so I really can't say. I have absolutely no idea. I was a member of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia. I was never excluded from the league so I'm -- I remain a member.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you work in Visoko, in logistics?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, we would need more time, not because of the witness but because of the OTP which expands, which broadens the issues with every witness. They give the entire history of the conflict, whereas the witness knows only of one part of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think we dealt with these issues. You are minded to tender 1D4260. Should we go into private session briefly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Gaynor, you have redirect examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I do, Mr. President, on simply one point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, the point is the Serb who sought shelter in your barracks. Today at page 47, Mr. Karadzic put a question to you: "Were there any Serbs who had sought shelter in your barracks or was it just Muslims? In your answer you said: "Among the first group of refugees, there was a Serb. He was a relative of a school friend of mine, Stojan. His name was Ivan. And he was among the first ones to arrive. He remained there the entire" --

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: Ljuban.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: That man Ljuban, do you know his surname?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: Blagojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Is he still alive?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: I don't know that. He was taken together with -- or rather, when the barracks was taken, he was taken together with us in a car.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Did you ever have a conversation with his brother after these events, while you were at KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: No. I only saw him for a moment, and he was surprised to see me in Velecevo. That's all there was there. We never saw each other afterwards. I never saw him after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Perhaps, could you confirm for me, yes or no, whether there was a Serb who took refuge with the Muslim refugees because he was helping Muslims in Foca?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Do you recall what happened to that Serb?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: He was also arrested.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Do you know if he is still alive?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-379
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Very well. I won't pursue the matter, Your Honours. No further questions in redirect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. That concludes your evidence at the Tribunal. On behalf of this Chamber, as well as the Tribunal as a whole, I'd like to thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now, you are free to go. Please have a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence is also very grateful to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will rise together. We will take a break for half an hour and resume at 20 past 5.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. President. First, we would like to introduce Marko Mrkonjic who has been working as an intern with our Case Managers, and today is his last day with our team so I would like to introduce him to you. Mr. President, the next issue we would like to raise involves the time for cross-examination of this next witness. I'm a little surprised that you thought it was untimely to raise the issue when we were at the end of the allotted time for cross-examination because usually you're telling us you want to wait and see and how things develop, but since -- if you prefer to hear the submissions now we would like to ask for more time for cross-examination of this next witness. And I can -- if you're ready to hear that, I can go into that right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, this witness testified in an earlier trial here in the Tribunal and the direct examination took approximately four hours. It's scheduled for another hour of direct examination here today, for a total of five hours, plus he was cross-examined for about one hour and 30 minutes on issues that are not particularly important to Dr. Karadzic because they involved one particular location in the municipality. And so we would ask that you -- you have given three hours, which is 60 per cent of the cross-examination, and we basically believe that it's not fair to give Dr. Karadzic less than the amount of the direct examination. For cross-examination you have to not only deal with material in direct but you raise issues of credibility, so in theory you need more time than for direct examination. And I don't see the Prosecution getting graded on performance in terms of the time for direct examination or redirect examination, and it seems somewhat unfair to Dr. Karadzic to give him below the time for direct examination by -- based on performance as opposed to telling him when something is irrelevant and making him move on to another area. Sometimes in my own experience and perhaps Judge Morrison has had the same experience, sometimes you hit gold in the last half hour of your cross-examination and it's, you know -- there can be unproductive cross-examination and productive cross-examination but an accused ought to have the time to be able to explore all the issues raised by the direct examination. So we would ask that you consider increasing the cross-examination time for this witness. I also have another issue with respect to the witness's protective measures and I would ask that we go into private session for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we deal with the first issue first?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff or Mr. Tieger, would you like to respond?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it's basically a matter for the Trial Chamber to address the request and I don't really want to make any submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, we have listened with interest to your submission, and in particular, the area where you referred to touching gold. Very interesting. At the moment, we are going to let the figure that we have awarded stand, but we shall most certainly consider your submission, and depending on the situation we will get back to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: There is one issue I've dealt with before and, Dr. Karadzic, I address you. I think it's worth repeating. In the first place, in relation to that which Mr. Robinson said about a nugget of gold in cross-examination, I do confess that I once cross-examined somebody for several hours without effect and my last question to him was that he was lying and he looked at the floor and he looked up at me and he said, Well, just a little bit. So I felt I had got somewhere. But on a much more serious note, it is, and I remind you, it's not the Serbian people who are on trial in this case, it's you. And what I'm about to say is intended to help rather than to be seen as any form of a stricture. While of course we don't know exactly what your case is until we hear it, the thrust of your case should really be focused upon issues of law, in particular those that revolve around command and/or superior responsibility and any allegation of any joint offending. Now, I agree that sometimes it's necessary to challenge factual matters in that regard, but very often it isn't, and especially if the facts are not in reality contested to any significant degree. Questions of historical reasoning and provocation are almost always irrelevant to the case. So try to make your essential legal point first in cross-examination, and then any remaining time can be spent on what might be thought to be secondary issues. That is going to require a different focus on cross-examination than you usually employ, and for that reason, I don't expect you to be able to do it immediately. But my experience over the years, and I suspect Mr. Robinson's, that by dealing with the really central points first, you become a better cross-examiner and the cross-examination is often more effective and productive, and as a byproduct it's usually much shorter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Morrison. We have had that same discussion and in Dr. Karadzic's defence, he's told me that as a literary person who is a writer he's used to making a buildup and so it's a different way of working for him, but I think he understands and he's improved quite a bit. I just want to point out to everyone, you don't hear Dr. Karadzic making comments any more. That was a constant source of concern for the Chamber. And he has -- doesn't do that any more and I think that he does quite a good job of learning from these -- advice that he receives from the Chamber. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Every day in court is a learning process, Mr. Robinson, even for judges, so I take that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will hear from you on your next point. Shall we go into private session?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, let the witness be brought in.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While we are waiting for the witness, let me ask can we work in the afternoon tomorrow? I need half a day to prepare.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Practically, I don't think it's possible. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. Good afternoon, sir. Do you follow the proceedings in the language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I haven't understood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you hear me in the language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. If you could take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable. Sir, I would like to inform you, on behalf of the Chamber, that you'll be testifying today with the benefit of pseudonym, image and voice distortion. This means that there will be no reference to your real name or information which might reveal your identity to the public or media. The audiovisual record of your testimony, which is broadcast to the public, will have a distorted image, which you can see in front of you on the monitor. Shall we show it to the witness now. Like this. And distorted -- and image and distorted voice to ensure that your identity is protected, and the transcript, while available to the public, will always refer to your pseudonym, which is KDZ-239. Do you understand that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And are you -- you are happy with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-239
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we briefly have Exhibit 20788 displayed on the screen but not broadcast, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Sir, the name listed as the first, and the date below there, is this your name and is it your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-239
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is the pseudonym sheet used in the Krnojelac case, and I request the admittance of this exhibit and it needs to be under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. That will be done.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P3334, under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, you testified before this Tribunal in the case against Milorad Krnojelac on the 27th and 28th November, 2000; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-239
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to review this testimony when you prepared for your testimony in the current case?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-239
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can you affirm that the testimony accurately reflects the evidence you provided to the Tribunal in the year 2000?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-239
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, one correction needs to be made, only to the English transcript. In line 2, on page 1187, in a question, there is a reference to a Mr. Kovacic and what he said in relations to Muslims. The question is not about Mr. Kovacic, as it states here in the English transcript, it was about Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Is that correct, witness?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-239
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, would you provide that same evidence to the Court if questioned on the same matters here today?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-239
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, with the one correction I just made I would like to tender this testimony as 65 ter 20783 for admission under Rule 92 ter, and it needs to be under seal because there is a closed session part in it. A public version is uploaded as 65 ter 20783A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will admit both versions.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As 65 ter 20783 will be Exhibit P3335, under seal, and the redacted version, 20783A will be Exhibit P3336.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The pseudonym sheet we just saw earlier on contains other names, names of other protected witnesses, which can be redacted?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The pseudonym sheet here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we up load without broadcasting?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, it was without broadcasting and I had actually asked that it be admitted under seal. The references to the other witnesses refer to their names that are from the Krnojelac case, and in the Krnojelac case, the witness basically refers to these numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So we may need them --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We need them here as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- to understand the context.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. That will be done. We will leave it at that. Thank you, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you. With the Court's permission I would now read a brief summary of the witness's evidence as admitted. Witness KDZ-239 lived in Foca and observed the political developments before the outbreak of the conflict and heard speeches by politicians of the SDS such as that Serbs can no longer live with the Muslims. Shortly after the attack on Foca by Serb forces, the witness was arrested and first detained in the hangar of the former TO warehouse in Livade and then at the Foca KP Dom prison. Among the non-Serbs detained in the various hangars of the TO warehouse in Livade were women and children. While detained at Livade, the witness observed looting and destruction of houses inhabited by Muslims. While detained in the KP Dom, the witness observed the mistreatment of detainees and noticed the effect the abuse and the living conditions, in particular, the hangar and the coldness, had on the physical and psychological health of the detainees. The detainees were civilians including old and sick people and doctors. Due to the living conditions and the lack of proper medical treatment and care, several detainees died in the prison. The witness observed the pattern of interrogations in the administration building of the KP Dom. In particular, in summer 1992, he saw and heard the beatings and killings of detainees. Detainees had to perform forced labour in the KP Dom and outside, and some were hidden from the Red Cross when it came to visit the prison. The witness observed the disappearance of detainees in so-called exchanges. The witness had contacts with Milorad Krnojelac, the warden of the KP Dom, who told him that the prison staff acted on orders from a superior command. Krnojelac told him that there were detention facilities in all municipalities, and the witness found this confirmed after he was transferred from the Foca KP Dom to the Kula prison in 1993. The witness was detained at the Kula prison for about one year, and he observed that detainees were wounded and killed when being taken out for forced labour. Your Honour, that concludes the summary. And I have now a few questions to ask in addition. Can we please have the transcript of intercept 30532 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And as it is coming up, witness, did you have an opportunity to listen to an intercept when preparing for your testimony?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-239
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you recognise any of the voices?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-239
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Whom did you recognise?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-239
utterances.text: I recognised the voice of Miro Stanic, president of the SDS in Foca, and Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And how familiar are you with the voice of Miro Stanic? Did you know him from before the war?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-239
utterances.text: Yes. I knew him well.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And you said that he was the president of the SDS in Foca. Do you know who had this position -- do you know who had this position before Mr. Stanic became the president?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-239
utterances.text: Yes. It was Mr. Petko Cancar.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And looking at the intercept transcript that we have here in front of you, there is in the lower part of the B/C/S version, there is a reference to problems in relation to Momcilo Mandic. Do you know what the problems with Mr. Mandic were in January 1992?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-239
utterances.text: Yes. It was a purely private problem of Mr. Mandic's, and I don't think that at that point in time it had anything to do with politics. At that time he was minister of justice in Republika Srpska. However --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me interrupt you here. That's actually sufficient. We do not need to go into details, more details, right now.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we please have the next page in both languages? In the lower part in the B/C/S, and in the English in the middle, there is a reference, Dr. Karadzic is asking, "Can they introduce independence in Foca?" And, "No,"-- and Stanic says, "No, they won't. The journalist from the 'Spiegel' were here yesterday." And he says, "So we told them we will never allow that." And then he also says, "We have formed a Serb municipality and you have that information."

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, do you know what this refers to?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-239
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-239
utterances.text: Yes. It has to do with the decision of the SDS of BH to establish a Serb Municipality of Foca.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I request this to be MFIed according to the procedure here. It's at the moment MFIed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be MFI P3337.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we please have Exhibit 65 ter 01412 on the screen. And as it is coming up, it is a radio report of 14 April 1992, with Velibor Ostojic reporting from Foca. If you can zoom in in the B/C/S on the upper part?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Sir, when you reviewed this short report when preparing for your testimony, did you find a mistake in there related to the location mentioned here as Ladja?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-239
utterances.text: Could that question please be repeated?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When you look at the reference here, it is -- it says here in this document, it says, in the middle, "It is continuing in Donje Polje with several pockets of activity towards Ladja and Celovina." What does Ladja refer to?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-239
utterances.text: I think that it hasn't been recorded properly. I think the proper recording would be Aladza.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And Aladza, is that a neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-239
utterances.text: Yes. What is meant here is a neighbourhood called Aladza but then there is also this mosque in this neighbourhood called Aladza mosque.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, can you help us with the sky-scraper Mr. Ostojic is talking about here? He speaks about a sky-scraper with a sniper nest. Do you know where it is situated and who was living there in this sky-scraper?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-239
utterances.text: Yes. This sky-scraper was between the Aladza local commune and the local commune of Donje Polje. Both Muslims and Serbs lived in it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to have this document admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P3338, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I would now like to have Exhibit 65 ter 17234 be brought up on the screen. And as it is coming up, it is a certificate dated 4th June 1992, referring to the decision of the Presidency of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina to establish war commissions in municipalities and the certificate refers to Professor Dr. Maksimovic being appointed to state commissioner for the Foca municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, this is a document where someone signs on behalf of the president of the Presidency, Dr. Radovan Karadzic. If you look at the signature, can you read who is signing for Dr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-239
utterances.text: I think it was Nikola Koljevic that signed it. Nikola Koljevic, in Cyrillic. For the president.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Thank you. Do you know Vojislav Maksimovic?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-239
utterances.text: Yes, I know him well.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was he from Foca?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-239
utterances.text: Yes. He was born in the village of Cvilin, and a bigger town close to that village is Ustikolina. He was held in high regard in that local commune. The majority of the population there was Muslim, 70 per cent. He was held in very high regard as a citizen and professor. What was depressing for people from that location, from that area, were Mr. Maksimovic's statements at the SDS meeting in Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What did he say there that depressed the people?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-239
utterances.text: He said, by way of his own rhetoric, that in the previous war the Drina flowed bloody, and in this war the Cehotina river would flow bloody too, and that indeed came true.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It states further here in the certificate, it says this certificate shall supersede the authority previously vested in Velibor Ostojic who had been given new tasks and duties. Sir, do you know Velibor Ostojic also from Foca?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-239
utterances.text: Yes. I know him, not as well as Maksimovic, but I do know him. He was born in Celebici, 45 kilometres away from Foca. It's almost at the border with Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to have this document admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P3339, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, in the testimony in the Krnojelac case, you gave quite a lot of details on the prison staff and we do not need to repeat all these details. I would just like to show you one exhibit, and this is number 1 -- 65 ter 14942, and can this be please on the screen. We have here a decision of the Executive Board of the Foca municipality related to work obligation and it is signed by Mr. Mladjenovic, who -- he signs here for -- as president of the Executive Board. Do you know Mr. Mladjenovic, and do you know whether he held such a position?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-239
utterances.text: Yes. I know Mr. Mladjenovic. He was a professor at a school. As for this position, president of the Executive Board, he held that in the joint assembly of the Muslims and Serbs in Foca that had been constituted on the 25th of December, 1990.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Looking at point 3 in this document, could we please zoom in a bit on the B/C/S in particular so that the witness can see it. And it says here, the Crisis Staff of the Serb Municipality of Foca and the command of the JNA unit shall engage the workers from the previous item if needed and required by the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Sir, this work obligation, how does it relate to the KP Dom staff? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-239
utterances.text: Yes. All of them, guards, policemen, it's synonymous, who worked in the previous system were assigned to work there. It's called work obligation here. But that does not rule out going to the front line. It's a group of some 37 to 40 previous employees, people who worked as policemen, that is.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I would like to have this admitted, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P3340, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, you mentioned that Mr. Krnojelac and other prison authorities referred to the superior command and that they would just execute the orders of that superior command. As a reference, it is in page 1172 of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we please, in this context, have 65 ter 07332 on the screen. And as it is coming up, it is a request by the commander, Miro Stanic, of the command of the tactical group Foca of 8 May 1992, to make available rooms in the KP Dom for prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Sir, can you remind us from when people were detained in the KP Dom? I mean in the war situation, not before the war.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-239
utterances.text: People who were detained were kept in building 1 and building 2. Those were the numbers assigned to these buildings.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And can you tell us since when, from when onwards were people detained in the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-239
utterances.text: I was transferred to the KP Dom in the evening on the 17th of April, 1992. As they were bringing us in, I found quite a few people there from Donje Polje for the most part. This is a Muslim area that is the closest to KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much. It refers here in this document to prisoners of war. Were you and the many other detainees in the KP Dom prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-239
utterances.text: No, no. Civilians only. They took us prisoner at our places of work, in the streets, in our homes. Some people were hiding in the woods, and then they found them there and brought them to the KP Dom. At any rate, no one was there who had been at the front line.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to have this document admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P3341, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we please have Exhibit 65 ter 07665 on the screen? And as it is coming up, it's a response by Mr. Krnojelac complying with this request basically.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, did anything change at that time for the detainees? You mentioned it was starting in April and now we have the 8th of May. Does anything change at that time?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-239
utterances.text: No. On the contrary, things got worse.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we briefly have document P01141 on the screen. It's already an exhibit in evidence, Your Honour. And we have here a decision of the minister of justice, Mr. Mandic, appointing Milorad Krnojelac on the 17th of July, 1992, to be the warden.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, did the conditions for the detainees in any way change from mid-July 1992?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-239
utterances.text: No. The bad situation escalated in every way, in terms of our health and survival.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we please have Exhibit 65 ter 16261 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In the meantime, we can admit 7665.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P3342, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: As it is here now, there is another decision of Mr. Mandic dated 16 December 1992, appointing Savo Todovic to acting deputy warden, and we do not go into details on Savo Todovic -- it says here "Todorovic." I can't read the B/C/S. There is a mistake at least in the English. What does it say in the B/C/S in relation to the name of the lawyer from Foca being appointed deputy warden?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-239
utterances.text: Todovic, Savo.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, the name is misspelled here in this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. That's noted.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And now, giving the date December 1992, did Todovic's position vis-à-vis the detainees change at that time, in any way?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-239
utterances.text: No. Well, this was post festum. I mean the decision came after his de facto appointment.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I request the admission of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that will be admitted as Exhibit P3343.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Witness in your previous testimony you gave a great many details on the detainees in the KP Dom and their fate. We do not go into this detail again.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: But can we please have Exhibit 65 ter 06929 on the screen. And it is here already in the B/C/S. It is a note by Krnojelac to the Crisis Staff of the -- of 15 May 1992, forwarding a release request of a detainee Enes Zekovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Sir, do you know this detainee? Was he indeed detained there and then released?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-239
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Who was he and why was he there detained?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-239
utterances.text: Like everyone else, except he was a Muslim and probably he had a different kind of political affiliation. He used to work for the municipality of Foca before the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you know why you were detained there?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-239
utterances.text: The reasons were the same for most of us civilians, detainees. Just because we were Muslims, because we had a different faith. And a number also had a different political affiliation. However, an enormous number of people who happened to be there were not interested in politics at all or political parties. There were sick people there. They were not interested in anything. They could not really orient themselves. There were really quite a few people like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I request the admission of this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P3344, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we please have Exhibit 65 ter 14848 on the screen. And as it is coming up, it's only partly readable, but it is a list of persons to be released from KP Dom, from May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And Mr. Witness, do you know these people or some of them, and were they in fact released?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-239
utterances.text: Yes. I know them. And for a longish period of time, they were there. The camp was officially opened on the 18th and then until the 5th of May, well that would be the period that they spent there. And as we can see, all of them are elderly people, exhausted, full of fear. They were there for a while. But when they were released, when they were allowed to go home, as it says there, they were supposed to report every day to the public security station of Foca.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And at the end, it says here that they have been operatively processed. We don't have the English right now here but it says so in the last line. Do you know what that means "operatively processed"?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-239
utterances.text: What I see on the screen is what it says down here, reasons are the illness and age of all the mentioned persons, ah, yes, it does say operatively processed. It's barely legible. That means that they were interrogated by the police in the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I request the admission of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be MFI P3345, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just was told the English is there now so you have an English version now in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We take your word. That will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you. I thought you had it. Thank you. I would now like to have Exhibit 65 ter 14742 on the screen, and I hope it's now there in both languages. It's another list of persons to be released.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this please be enlarged a bit?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, so we have now both languages and it is a list of people to be released without interrogation, dated the 9th of May, 1992. Do you know these people listed here?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-239
utterances.text: Yes. I know all of them. For a long time I lived in Miljevina, for over 15 years with my family. So I knew people well. And I could deal with them one by one. But I would immediately like to deal with person number 13.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, we need to go into private session for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. May the Chamber move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And the other people listed here, do you know whether they are -- were in fact released and are alive or not?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-239
utterances.text: I'm not sure that all of them were in KP Dom, that all of them were brought there. I don't remember the person under number 13, but I know that Subasic, Mirsad was there. He was a young man, around 25 years old, and also it's not Dzanko Senad but rather two brothers, Elmedin and Eldin. They were also younger people and I saw them in the KP Dom. As for the others, I'm not sure. What I'm sure about though is that none of them are alive nowadays and haven't been alive for a long time.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I would like to have this document admitted, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P3346, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: One more document, I would like to have 65 ter 14944 be brought on to the screen. And as it is coming up, it is an order by commander Marko Kovac dated the 7th September 1992, related to the arrest of suspects and their release.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you know what this order is related to?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-239
utterances.text: This is an order of the commander of the Foca Brigade, Colonel Marko Kovac, who ordered the administration of KP Dom, how they were to release people, under what conditions, and whom they could release.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And to what type of detainees would that relate? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-239
utterances.text: Yes. This pertained exclusively to civilians.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I request the admission of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P3347, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Sir, in your testimony, you only very briefly described the situation of the detainees in Kula prison and you refer to people getting wounded and killed while doing work outside of the prison, and it's at the end of the testimony in chief at 1285. And you refer to a particular incident in January 1994 when several people were taken out very early in the morning for work and two got killed. Mr. Witness, do you remember the persons, the two persons, that were killed?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-239
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I can say that -- I can say the names of those people, or I can tell you where they were from.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Please tell us the names and also where they were from.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-239
utterances.text: One of those who were killed was Mesudin Smaic. And the other was a younger person from the village of Grapska. I can't remember his first or last name. However, he was an artisan, and he worked at the chicken farm in Kula because in Kula, I found a number of prisoners from Doboj, Banja Luka, Grapska, from the camps around Sarajevo and Pale. And this is what confirmed the statement of Milorad on the 10th of June when he talked to me, namely that there were camps throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina under the control of Serb forces. At the end, he told me, We don't know what to do now.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And this person Mesudin Smaic, where -- when did he arrive in the Kula prison, and how?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-239
utterances.text: Mesudin Smaic and his brother Hasudin Smaic arrived after a complete ethnic cleansing in the municipality of Rogatica. They arrived in a larger group, in two or three buses. They entered the compound of the Kula camp. There were a number of elderly people there, women and some five or six children.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, this concludes the examination-in-chief. I request the admission of the associated exhibits listed in the first table of the appendix to the 92 ter notification.
